expectedText:
PHASE-IN OVERTIME FOR AGRICULTURAL WORKERS ACT (LABOR CODE §§ 857-864) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND DECLARATION
This document sets out information about California's Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016, Labor Code sections 857 through 864, prepared in connection with work performed for Acme, Inc. by Jordan Lee in the position of Field Supervisor, beginning on or about March 1, 2026. This document describes what the statute itself provides, including a graduated phase-in schedule that has now fully taken effect under the statute's own terms. It is not legal advice about how the statute applies to any particular person's specific work arrangement, hours, or duties.

STATUTORY TITLE AND LEGISLATIVE FINDINGS
Labor Code Chapter 6, sections 857 through 864, located within the Division 2 working-hours provisions, is titled and may be cited as the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016. It was added by Assembly Bill 1066 (Statutes 2016, Chapter 313), effective January 1, 2017. In enacting the chapter, the Legislature found that agricultural workers had historically been excluded from wage and overtime protections under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, and it declared its intent to give persons employed in an agricultural occupation in California an opportunity to earn overtime compensation under the same standards as other Californians.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 857 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=857.&lawCode=LAB)
  "In 1938, the United States Congress enacted the federal Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 201 et seq.), which excluded agricultural workers from wage protections and overtime compensation requirements."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 858(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=858.&lawCode=LAB)
  "It is the intent of the Legislature to enact the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016 to provide any person employed in an agricultural occupation in California, as defined in Order No. 14-2001 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (revised 07-2014) with an opportunity to earn overtime compensation under the same standards as millions of other Californians."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 858(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=858.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes the chapter's title provision (section 857) and its legislative findings and declaration of intent (section 858); it does not restate every finding listed in section 858, only the findings quoted below. These findings are legislative background statements, not independently operative rules, and by themselves they do not establish an overtime entitlement; the operative overtime and double-time rules are set out in sections 860 through 862, addressed in separate clauses in this document.

DEFINITION OF "AGRICULTURAL OCCUPATION"
Chapter 6 applies to a person "employed in an agricultural occupation." The chapter does not itself define that phrase. Instead, section 859 provides that "employed in an agricultural occupation" has the same meaning given to it in Wage Order No. 14-2001 of California's Industrial Welfare Commission, as revised effective July 2014. Section 858 refers to the same source when describing the chapter's intended coverage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For purposes of this chapter, “employed in an agricultural occupation” has the same meaning as in Order No.14-2001 of the Industrial Welfare Commission (revised 07-2014)."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 859 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=859.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This document quotes only Chapter 6's own cross-reference to Wage Order No. 14-2001; it does not independently fetch, quote, or verify the text of Wage Order No. 14-2001 itself, which is a separate Industrial Welfare Commission order rather than a Labor Code section, and was not checked against leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as part of this research. Determining whether a specific job duty falls within "agricultural occupation" as the Wage Order defines it would require consulting that Wage Order directly, which this document does not do.

THE SECTION 860 PHASE-IN SCHEDULE AND ITS CURRENT, FULLY-EFFECTIVE STATUS
Labor Code section 860 set out a graduated schedule under which persons employed in an agricultural occupation became entitled to daily and weekly overtime pay on a step-down basis, moving toward the general 8-hour-per-day/40-hour-per-week overtime threshold that already applied to most other California nonexempt employees. For most agricultural employers, the daily/weekly threshold stepped down in four stages: 9.5 hours per day or 55 hours per week beginning January 1, 2019; 9 hours per day or 50 hours per week beginning January 1, 2020; 8.5 hours per day or 45 hours per week beginning January 1, 2021; and 8 hours per day or 40 hours per week beginning January 1, 2022. The statute set the same four-stage schedule, delayed by three years at each stage, for an employer that employs 25 or fewer employees, with that group's final 8-hour/40-hour stage beginning January 1, 2025. Because January 1, 2025 has passed, section 860's phase-in schedule has now run its full course for both employer-size groups under the statute's own terms, and the 8-hour-workday/40-hour-workweek threshold is the daily/weekly overtime threshold that section 860 currently states for agricultural occupations covered by this chapter, without regard to employer size.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Commencing January 1, 2019, except as provided in paragraph (2), any person employed in an agricultural occupation shall not be employed more than nine and one-half hours in any one workday or work in excess of 55 hours in any one workweek, unless the employee receives one and one-half times that employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over nine and one-half hours in any workday or over 55 hours in any workweek."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 860(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=860.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Commencing January 1, 2022, except as provided in paragraph (2), any person employed in an agricultural occupation shall not be employed more than eight hours in any one workday or work in excess of 40 hours in any one workweek, unless the employee receives one and one-half times that employee’s regular rate of pay for all hours worked over eight hours in any workday or over 40 hours in any workweek."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 860(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=860.&lawCode=LAB)
  "This subdivision shall apply to an employer who employs 25 or fewer employees commencing January 1, 2025."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 860(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=860.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause summarizes all four stages of section 860's schedule for both employer-size categories from a single statutory section; it is not corroborated by an independent second source. Section 863 gave the Governor limited authority, under specified conditions tied to a minimum-wage-increase suspension mechanism, to delay this schedule by up to one year at a time; this document did not research whether the Governor ever exercised that authority for this chapter, so this clause describes the schedule as enacted rather than independently confirming that no delay in fact occurred. This document does not address how "employs 25 or fewer employees" is counted (for example, over what period, or across what related entities), because Chapter 6 does not itself define that counting method.

EXTENSION OF GENERAL OVERTIME RULES AND THE 12-HOUR DOUBLE-TIME THRESHOLD
Labor Code section 861 provides that, except for the daily/weekly thresholds set out in section 860 and the 12-hour daily double-time threshold set out in section 862(a), all other provisions of California's general overtime statute (Labor Code Chapter 1, commencing with section 500) governing compensation for overtime work apply to workers in an agricultural occupation, effective January 1, 2017. Separately, section 862(a) sets a 12-hour-per-day double-time threshold for agricultural occupations, stated as "consistent with Section 510," California's general double-time statute: work beyond 12 hours in one day is compensated at no less than twice the employee's regular rate of pay. Section 862 phased this 12-hour double-time threshold in on the same two-track, employer-size-based schedule used in section 860: it began applying January 1, 2022 for other employers, and, for an employer that employs 25 or fewer employees, beginning January 1, 2025. Because January 1, 2025 has passed, the 12-hour daily double-time threshold in section 862(a) is now the double-time threshold that section 862 currently states for agricultural occupations covered by this chapter, without regard to employer size.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as set forth in Section 860 and subdivision (a) of Section 862, all other provisions of Chapter 1 (commencing with Section 500) regarding compensation for overtime work shall apply to workers in an agricultural occupation commencing January 1, 2017."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 861 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=861.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Beginning January 1, 2022, except as provided in subdivision (c), and consistent with Section 510, any work performed by a person, employed in an agricultural occupation, in excess of 12 hours in one day shall be compensated at the rate of no less than twice the employee’s regular rate of pay."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 862(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=862.&lawCode=LAB)
  "Subdivision (a) shall apply to an employer who employs 25 or fewer employees commencing January 1, 2025."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 862(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=862.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause draws on sections 861 and 862(a) and (c), which are provisions of the same statutory chapter and are not independent sources of one another. This document does not independently trace how the general seventh-consecutive-workday double-time rule in Labor Code section 510(a) (extended to agricultural occupations by section 861's reference to "other provisions" of the general overtime chapter) interacts with section 862's 12-hour daily double-time rule for this specific worker category; that interaction is not addressed here.

THE GOVERNOR'S NOW-LAPSED AUTHORITY TO DELAY THE PHASE-IN
Labor Code section 863 gave the Governor limited, conditional authority to temporarily suspend the scheduled phase-in of the overtime and double-time requirements in sections 860 and 862(a), but only if the Governor also suspended a scheduled minimum-wage increase under a specified, cross-referenced provision of Labor Code section 1182.12. Any such suspension could postpone the schedule by at most one additional year at a time, and section 863 fixed an outer limit on how long this suspension authority could exist: it stated that the authority would end once the final phase-in steps described in section 860(d) and section 862(c) took effect, or on January 1, 2025, whichever came first.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding Section 860 or 862, the Governor may temporarily suspend scheduled phase in of the overtime requirements set forth in Section 860, or subdivision (a) of Section 862 only if the Governor suspends scheduled minimum wage increases pursuant to clause (i) of subparagraph (A) of, and subparagraph (B) of, paragraph (3) of subdivision (d) of Section 1182.12."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 863(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=863.&lawCode=LAB)
  "The Governor’s authority to suspend the scheduled overtime requirements under this section shall end upon the phase in of the overtime requirements contained in subdivision (d) of Section 860, the phase in of the overtime requirements contained in subdivision (c) of Section 862, or January 1, 2025, whichever occurs first."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 863(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=863.&lawCode=LAB)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from section 863 alone. This document did not research, and does not state, whether the Governor ever exercised this suspension authority during the phase-in period; it addresses only the authority as fixed in the statutory text and the fact that the statute's own end-date for that authority, January 1, 2025, has now passed. This document does not describe the separate minimum-wage-suspension mechanism under Labor Code section 1182.12 that section 863 cross-references, beyond noting that it exists as a precondition to the Governor's authority under section 863.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT
By signing below, Acme, Inc. and Jordan Lee acknowledge that they have received and reviewed this information about the Phase-In Overtime for Agricultural Workers Act of 2016.

Employer: Acme, Inc.
Signed: ______________________ Date: September 5, 2026

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signed: ______________________ Date: September 5, 2026

Executed at Oakland, California.
